idiom_name: abstract factory interface + one concrete factory per family + abstract products
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare an interface with exactly one creation operation per product kind; implement it once per family so that each implementation instantiates the matching concrete products; have clients depend only on that interface and on the abstract product interfaces. Select the family once at a composition root (configuration key, environment, DI registration) and pass the factory instance down; never let client code branch on the family. Keep the factory interface small and stable, and split it into composed sub-factories if the number of product kinds keeps growing. Return ownership-explicit products (objects, handles or smart pointers) and document who releases them. The FamilySelector (or Registrar) role is the single call site where the family key is resolved and the concrete factory is instantiated; it belongs at the composition root, never in client code. For runtime factory loading (plugins, ServiceLoader), prefer a registry map of factory constructors over a switch on the family key.
code_sketch:
interface WidgetFactory:            # one operation per product KIND
    make_button(): Button
    make_slider(min, max): Slider

class DarkTheme implements WidgetFactory:
    make_button(): return DarkButton()      # only this class names Dark*
    make_slider(min, max): return DarkSlider(min, max)

# client
widgets = DarkTheme()                        # chosen once, at the composition root
form = [widgets.make_button(), widgets.make_slider(0, 100)]
pitfalls: Wrong move: let the client branch on the family key; failure: every consumer regains concrete-family coupling and new families require shotgun edits; instead: resolve the key once at the composition root and inject the factory.

Wrong move: share one factory instance whose family is changed by mutable state; failure: later clients silently receive a different family and concurrent requests race; instead: make the family immutable after construction or create one factory per scope.

Wrong move: keep adding product kinds to one wide factory; failure: every factory and client changes together and the interface becomes hard to test; instead: split role-specific sub-factories or choose a simpler creator.

Wrong move: return null or undefined for an unsupported product; failure: the wrong family propagates until a distant null dereference; instead: reject the family or fail fast with a descriptive construction error.

Wrong move: read a global flag, thread-local or ambient environment inside the factory; failure: tests cannot control selection independently and request isolation breaks; instead: pass an explicit family selector or factory from the composition root.

Wrong move: define the abstract factory in the library that owns concrete products; failure: clients depend on an abstraction optimized for the library rather than their use case; instead: let the client/application own the interface (Dependency Inversion Principle).
sources: Mark Seemann, 'Placement of Abstract Factories', ploeh blog (2014) — https://blog.ploeh.dk/2014/12/24/Placement-of-Abstract-Factories/
